speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Marshall (Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe) moved:
subsubtopic: TRANSFER OF WESTMINSTER HOSPITAL IN LONDON
speechtext:
That an humble address be presented to is Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House copies of all correspondence, minutes of meetings, telegrams, contracts and/or agreements between the government and the province of Ontario having to do with the transfer of Westminster Hospital in London.
December 2, 1976

He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to debate one of my motions for the production of papers No. 8, not merely because of the particular issue which is related to the concern over the effect on veterans involved but, more importantly, to emphasize the ridiculous situation that results when I am told that the material requested, referring to correspondence, minutes of meetings, telegrams, contracts and/or agreements between the federal government and the province of Ontario having to do with the transfer of Westminster hospital in London cannot be released because of ongoing discussions between the two governments.
The reason I request these papers is to try to prevent a recurrence of the failure of the Department of Veterans Affairs to project and plan for the needs of entitled veterans which is becoming more and more obvious as a result of the concern expressed by veterans and veterans groups after hospitals have already been transferred. I can only ask why I am being denied my right on behalf of veterans who have submitted their appeal to myself, my party and the minister, to have this information. The commitment by the minister or his predecessors has not been completely fulfilled. This commitment was made under cabinet decision on December 5, 1963, entitled "Medical treatment for veterans". It relates as follows:
A)	That the Department of Veterans Affairs be authorized to withdraw gradually from the operations of departmental hospitals, as opportunities arose to do so under conditions acceptable, and to turn these hospitals over to the operation of non-federal agencies for the benefit of the total community.
B)	The conditions acceptable to the department in making such a transfer of operational control would generally require:
1)	A guarantee of unconditional priority use of beds, either in the hospitals which were transferred or, in other suitable hospitals, for the treatment of service-incurred disabilities.
2)	Assurance of the existence in the community of adequate hospital resources to absorb the workload created by war veterans allowance recipients, and
3)	The requirement of satisfactory arrangements for the protection of the employment and pension status of civil servants now employed in veterans hospitals.
According to my records, there are 11 veterans' hospitals in Canada. Of these, five have been already transferred. I can only presume that the others are in the process of negotiation. But certainly it is obvious, through information I can receive from everyone else but the department involved, that Westminster is presently under negotiation for transfer. This brings me to the point of my motion: why am I refused the documents in my attempts to ensure by doing so that the mistakes in the past, as evidenced by the complaints being received over transfers, can be corrected by debate in this House? Why, indeed, am I refused freedom of information which is supposed to be of so much concern in this House of Commons? Why, indeed, is there so much secrecy involved if indeed, the minister feels that he is fulfilling his obligation to the Canadian veteran? I think he should look at some of the facts concerning those veterans who are involved.
The priority requirement at present is to provide adequate chronic and domiciliary beds for veterans. In almost all cases
Westminster Hospital
since the transfers this commitment has not been fulfilled to its fullest extent. Visits to a few of the hospitals by myself and some of my colleagues have borne this out. We have brought the matter to the attention of the minister. Let me make clear that we do not object to the policy of transfer. We recognize the reasons for the transfer. It is becoming increasingly difficult to maintain qualified personnel because as veterans grow older their need for care has shifted from acute to the extended care. But despite the best intentions of the minister, who I must admit is trying to correct the inadequate projections by his predecessors, it is becoming more and more obvious that the department has not been able to make practical arrangements for the required bed space for veterans' needs where hospitals have been turned over to the civilian authority.
The situation will become worse as World War II veterans reach the 70 and 80-year bracket over the next 20 years. This emphasizes the projected need for domiciliary care beds. I will deal with other hospital transfers at a later date. Referring to the Westminister Hospital alone, it is very obvious that the authorities of the hospital brought to the attention of the minister back in 1975 their concerns, because they are closer to hand and are more aware of what is going on in respect of their endeavours to care for the veterans in that hospital in London, Ontario. Let me read from a brief that was submitted in February 1975. It states:
For the past two years negotiations have been continuing between the Department of Veterans Affairs, the provincial government of Ontario and the London health planning board, for the transfer of Westminister Hospital to provincial control. The Federation of British Canadian Veterans are very concerned when policy of the federal government in any way affects the health and welfare of our aged ...
Various ministers of veterans affairs have stated time and again, that it is essential that the veterans' hospitals be turned over to local authorities, in order to maintain the high standard of treatment they have become accustomed to. The federation would be inclined to agree with this, in so far as active treatment is concerned, but not at the expense of the chronic, psychiatric and domiciliary care patients...
At this time-
That was in 1975, a year and a half ago.
-the Federation of British Canadian Veterans are more concerned with the future of the chronic, psychiatric and domiciliary care patients now in Westminister than with the proposed turnover.
Copies of this brief were presented to the veterans affairs committee at that time. The brief continues:
We have stated previously that our concern at this time was not the actual turnover of the hospital to municipal authorities but the future welfare of the chronic, psychiatric and domiciliary care patients. In order that we may further clarify the points in our resolution, we must first be assured that the members of the committee are aware of the lay-out of Westminister Hospital.
Since negotiations began between the Department of Veterans Affairs, the provincial government and the local health planning board, many reports have been publicized in the local press, the majority of which revealed little or nothing of the plans of either body, yet there was one very disturbing report, this calling for the transfer of the chronic, psychiatric and domiciliary care patients to the confines of Victoria Hospital. We, the Federation of British Canadian Veterans of Canada must take a definite stand against any such proposals ...
The Federation of British Canadian Veterans of Canada, after 30 years of dedication to serving our veterans, sincerely believe that here is a great opportunity for the federal government to set aside this little corner of this great land of ours as a memorial to all those courageous citizens, who during the many years of conflict gave their lives that we might live in freedom and peace.

December 2, 1976
Westminster Hospital
It is very strange that although this beautiful land will be transferred to a provincial government or a municipality at no cost, the federal government will have to provide the services from its capital fund which is needed so much to care for other veterans and their needs. The federation states:
1.	That we the Federation of British Canadian Veterans of Canada, request the federal government retain that part of Westminster Hospital, south of Commissioners Road and east of Wellington Road and it be so dedicated as a memorial to all those Canadians who have given their lives in the defence of our country.
2.	A new building be erected on the site, or the present psychiatric building be renovated to house the chronic, psychiatric and domiciliary care patients.
3.	A liaison be arranged with the local authorities so that patients needing active treatment may be transferred to the main hospital.
4.	The Department of Veterans Affairs retain supervision and control of all phases of treatment and care.
I indicated earlier in my remarks that I do not think past ministers or those who decided back in 1963 to transfer hospitals projected what would be needed at this time as conditions change. I did a little research. First may I refer to a letter I received from the minister dated September 17, 1976. This letter is vague. I asked the number of domiciliary care beds available in departmental institutions as of 1963. The letter indicates that between 1969 and 1976 there was not even an increase of 100 beds. As I said, with the number of Second World War veterans now at age 60 whose needs will increase over the next 10 or 20 years, this amazes me a bit. The minister says:
The number of section 29 VTR beds is not expected to vary appreciably in 1977 or 1978, except in the event that some hospitals are transferred.
I presume this letter was prepared for the minister by officials from the treatment services. The minister goes on to say in his letter:
It is expected that a sufficient number of beds will be reserved for domiciliary care patients as part of the agreement and will likely favour the veteran.
Do the minister and his staff not know how many beds will be needed? After extolling the virtues of doing all the things he says he will do, why does he say that the veterans will likely be favoured? We can show the minister lists of veterans across the country waiting for domiciliary and extended care. Commitments have been made to veterans, yet the minister only says that the veterans will likely be favoured. I have here some figures showing what the needs will be in the next 10 or 20 years. I have here the number of veterans receiving disability pensions. They now number 82,516. Over 12,000 of them are World War I veterans between the age of 75 and 80. There are 91,392 war veterans allowance recipients, and a great majority of the 173,908 veterans will be needing domiciliary care. I broke those figures down to the numbers receiving disability pensions of between 50 per cent and 100 per cent to point out that veterans in that category will likely need care. There are still 4,513 single World War I veterans between the ages of 75 and 80, most of them probably alone. The married World War I veterans number 7,869. It is obvious when the minister said that the department's projection for 1976 was for only 2,927 beds that somebody in his department must look again at those

projected figures, because we should be able to plan for the care of veterans.
The main object of this motion for the production of papers is to point out that I am being denied my right to provide help and assistance to veterans which I have done since I have been associated with veterans affairs in my party. We must never deny to the veteran the care which he deserves and to which prime ministers in the past 60 or 70 years have committed themselves.
I should like to quote from an article written by my colleague, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) which appeared in Reader's Digest. The caption reads: "It's all too easy for Ottawa to withhold the facts and data on which government decisions are made. But in a democracy, the public has as much right to know as the policymakers". It is obvious that the Westminster hospital is likely to be transferred very soon. The parliamentary secretary knows that all I want to do is to ensure, with the continued co-operation of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, that these veterans are looked after in accordance with the commitments made. The hon. member for Peace River referred in his article to another motion of mine when I sought documents about a meeting of senior officials to set a new deadline for loan applications under the Veterans Land Act. At that time the request was denied because the papers were confidential.
I put my case forward with all the sincerity and kindness which I feel toward veterans, and I know I will receive the co-operation of all hon. members regardless of party affiliation. I know that some of my colleagues will want to participate in the debate, and I apologize for taking up so much time.

speakeroldname: Mr. Victor S. Railton (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: TRANSFER OF WESTMINSTER HOSPITAL IN LONDON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that the minister was unable to attend at this time. I am sure he would have been very pleased to speak on the motion put forward by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). The minister cannot accede to the request of the hon. member for the tabling of all correspondence, minutes of meetings, telegrams, contracts and agreements between the povernment and the province of Ontario having to do with the transfer of Westminster hospital. The reason is that our officials have had meetings with the provincial authorities and have been unable to reach agreement to date. The situation at present is that the position is being re-examined, as the hon. member stated. The agreement is still under negotiation, and I hope we will be meeting soon with provincial officials.
The government feels strongly that it would be in the best interests of both veterans and the community to integrate Westminster into a planned complex of facilities at the present site. There may be some misconceptions even in the minds of people who are anxious to do their very best for veterans. I do not think we should have two classes of hospitals. Hospitals should provide the very best care for veterans whether it is geriatic care or acute hospital care. The hon. member must remember that the government's record with regard to the care of veterans in hospitals is very good indeed. Also, the government has been very anxious in all the negotiations also
December 2, 1976

to ensure proper care of the staff in these hospitals. So the possibility of keeping an area for domiciliary care at Westminster hospital may be very good indeed. For all I know, it may be under negotiation.
However, I think that the figures which the hon. member gave of the possible number of recipients of domiciliary care is somewhat larger than I think will be the case, because it is quite obvious that we can no longer look after all veterans in the veterans' hospitals. I think that a high level of care continues to be a prime requisite. In the case of Sunnybrook hospital, the level of care was declining until it was taken over. Now we have a 450-bed veterans' wing of which we can be proud and which veterans regard very highly. This wing provides chronic care, geriatric care or maybe extended care.
I think the hon. member will appreciate that this is the state of affairs in our discussions with the province. It would be quite irregular for the federal government unilaterally to hand out documents concerning the negotiations to date. That is pretty obvious. Nevertheless, this is a great opportunity to reiterate our position on the transfer of DVA hospitals. This was stated in a cabinet report of December 5, 1963. The report provides the terms of reference for all the negotiations concerning the transfer of hospitals.
Right after the last world war there were not enough hospitals in Canada to care for the wounded who were returning from overseas. Many of them came off hospital ships. Many were on stretchers and they had to go right to hospital. We had to have special hospitals built, and at one time we had 40 institutions. These were acute care cases requiring every conceivable kind of specialized care. They stayed in hospital for varying lengths of time. Some never got out of hospital. Many were discharged but had to return for treatment periodically. As the wounded veterans returned to health, the institutions were gradually closed down, but there were First World War and Second World War veterans who still required care of one kind or another so certain hospitals were kept open all across Canada. As the number of patients being treated for war wounds decreased, we began to allow the use of the beds for veterans such as war veterans allowance recipients.
These hospitals were never intended for this kind of use, and I think veterans should realize that. The beds were there, so we used them, and eventually we ended up with most of them being occupied by patients in need of care for chronic conditions frequently of a geriatric nature. It became harder and harder to attract young professional staff, both doctors and nurses, to work in the hospitals. They told us, with some justification, that the work was too limited. The young specialists wanted to work where they could experience the widest possible range of medical practice.
What happened when one of the veteran patients in what has become essentially a geriatric hospital suddenly needed acute care? The hospital did not have the staff to treat him. He had to be transferred. We could see this situation looming on the medical horizon so we got contracts with provincial
Westminster Hospital
authorities to transfer the hospitals to provincial jurisdiction. They have been integrated with local hospitals, but with certain guarantees for veterans. These guarantees included a specific number of beds reserved for veterans with pensionable disabilities. We were assured that there would be adequate care for war veterans allowance recipients, and the protection of the employment of hospital staff. I mentioned this just a while ago. The hon. member can appreciate that I am only giving a broad outline of the policy and I have not gone into the cost factors or the effect of hospital insurance on the transfer of responsibility. How many graduating doctors or nurses would choose a workplace which would limit their future? Hon. members can understand the difficulty in attracting competent staff, although this work would be good experience for every young man proceeding to specialty training.
I will ask the hon. member another question. If his father or brother suffered a heart attack, where would he take them-to a veterans hospital or to a modern local hospital? It has been proved time and again that modern local hospitals are better fitted to deal with acute illnesses and major surgery.
Our concern has been to provide the best possible care for veterans. That is why we continue to support and promote the hospital transfer policy. We are not avoiding our responsibilities to our veterans. We are doing everything in our power to give our veterans the kind of care and treatment they deserve. If the hon. member would look into this question, he would find it sometimes becomes a question of misconception. I have used the minister's notes to show how sincere we are in wanting to give veterans the very best care.
Now that this debate has been initiated by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe, I think there will be better understanding in Canada, especially by veterans, of the role of the federal government and the Department of Veterans Affairs in looking after our sick veterans.

subsubtopic: TRANSFER OF WESTMINSTER HOSPITAL IN LONDON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I wish to indicate how pleased I am to second the motion of the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) for the laying of these important documents before the House. I was somewhat concerned about some of the observations made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Railton) in giving his reasons for not producing these documents. He implied that there has not been agreement between the various parties in negotiating the transfer of jurisdiction of Westminster Hospital to some other prime complex in that particular area, although he did not define that specifically.
He talked about some of the misconceptions which have arisen because of these activities. That is the very reason the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe asked for the production of these papers. There is a need for this information. It might allay the fears and apprehensions of the veterans in that area, and there is also a necessity to have an input from those veterans. I have some personal background with respect to that. Some of my training was done at Westminster Hospital. I have looked after patients over a number of years who

December 2, 1976
Westminster Hospital
have utilized the splendid facilities at that hospital. A number of veterans from that area have expressed to me a number of concerns and it is only fair that I should share some of those concerns with the House because to me they form the crux of the problem. That is why I believe the production of these papers might allay some of those apprehensions and fears.
The major concern of the veterans in the area is the quality of medical care. They recognize that in years gone by they received excellent medical care at Westminster Hospital. They feel very comfortable in the surroundings there. They know the personnel; many individuals and veterans have been patients on a recurring basis for a number of years. The crux of the problem for them is the need to be reassured about the quality of the medical care they will have in the future.
There is some concern because of the government's initiative in introducing Bill C-68. They are well aware that the federal government has indicated it is prepared to reduce its fiscal responsibility with respect to health services in the provinces. They are concerned about whether that quality of care will be maintained in subsequent years. Very clearly there is uncertainty about the quality of medical care and whether it will be provided in some other area in the future.
Another concern expressed to me on numerous occasions is the question of where these veterans will be transferred to. Some of them honestly believe that they might be transferred to such distant areas as Toronto. It is quite obvious that these individuals want to be as close to their home as they can, whether that be Wallaceburg, Bothwell, Oil Springs, Blenheim, Ridgetown or many of the small communities which are at a distance close enough for their families to visit them.
The parliamentary secretary referred to a misconception, and this has not been defined, but there has been the suggestion that some of these veterans might be returned to local hospitals. No one is objecting to that concept in principle, but there is concern that some of these local hospitals might not have the facilities required for the special type of treatment veterans need, whether it be in the area of rehabilitation or whatever. It is important to have these papers so that we know the background and can allay the fears and apprehensions of veterans, especially veterans in that area.
I must also compliment the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe for raising the specific issue of chronic care and domiciliary-type cases, an issue which, without doubt, is of great concern to veterans in my area as well as to veterans all across Canada. We have seen no documented evidence to show that the government has a plan for meeting this particular need, which will grow in years to come. I again say to the parliamentary secretary that we urgently need to have this information tabled in the House of Commons so that we may know precisely what the government has in mind for chronic care and domiciliary-type cases.
Around the middle of September at a meeting held near Sarnia the possible closing down of Westminster Hospital or the transfer of patients, and the full implication of such closing

or transfer, were discussed. Unfortunately I must report to the House that the proceedings at that meeting did not allay the apprehension and fears of veterans in my area. After that meeting I received representations from veterans and it was evident that their fears had not been allayed, but were greater than ever.
May I refer again to the special services provided at Westminster Hospital? There is no indication-and this is why the pertinent documents ought to be tabled in the House-that special services for veterans, for example such as occupational therapy and rehabilitation, will be provided elsewhere. Therefore we need far greater assurance that veterans will continue to receive the particular kind of care to which they have been accustomed in the past.
Allow me to cite some more examples of special needs, Mr. Speaker. Let me say while I am on my feet that I am not unfamiliar with veterans' hospitals and extended care for veterans. I say with pride that after my father returned from Vimy Ridge where he had been seriously wounded he spent many days in veterans' hospitals. He had suffered from brain damage and had seriously injured his arm, which led to the loss of use of his hand and the loss of fingers. He became a totally disabled veteran. In those days the kind of care which is prevalent today was not available; not a great deal could be done for veterans in our hospitals. Finally, on his own initiative, my father took the leather braces which had been supplied to him and, in front of me-I was then a young boy eight or nine years old- threw off those braces. Although he was in terrible pain he took them off. I remember what happened.
Actually I think the Department of Veterans Affairs should analyse the experiences of veterans' children because possibly such an analysis would reveal much pertinent information about veterans.
If I may return to my father-he put himself to work and rehabilitated himself; and although classed as a totally disabled veteran he proved to himself that he could do many useful things. Mr. Speaker, I saw my beloved father going through the stage of almost howling, of crying with pain in the hallways in hospital, of screaming like a child in pain. That is why I sympathize with veterans. I remember as a boy going to St. Anne's to see my father. I used to crawl under the beds and I remember seeing the veterans who were then in baths of oil. Because of my experiences I still visit hospitals and, because of my father's experiences, I am able to sympathize with veterans in hospitals. For that reason I do not think that I look at these matters in a bureaucratic or technical way.
Having considered this general situation I have drawn the ultimate conclusion concerning the extended care a patient requires. In the interest of good treatment, a patient's extended care should be within a health care system geared to look after all his needs, no matter what direction his health may take. In other words he needs to be in a system which at any moment of day or night can call on the full range of professional medical care facilities. That cannot be organized in an extended care hospital which is not tightly integrated into a total community health care system.
Westminster Hospital
When you ask people making decisions in the area of health to produce papers, you are asking for details of a most confidential nature concerning those under treatment. Surely we will not treat our veterans in that manner. Our veterans, having given almost all but their lives for their country, would object to being treated as second-class citizens. Hon. members know that there have been objections concerning which hospital door veterans were to use. Now that improved health care facilities are available, particularly for extended care in hospitals, it may be necessary to make certain transfers, and I say that one should not make available documents which could be interpreted publicly to the possible disadvantage of those involved.
I wish to summarize in point form, if I may. First we must recognize that DVA hospitals were created to deal with the influx of returning war wounded. That was the idea. They were there to receive those lame souls when they returned.
As the wounded were brought back to health, beds became surplus and most of the institutions were closed. This has been a continuing process. As the number of pensioners in our remaining hospitals diminished, WVA recipients were admitted because beds were available and, to the extent that beds were available, this was a way to reduce the financial pressure on recipients in the days before hospital insurance.
The number of beds available for WVA recipients, however, has diminished as we ceased operating hospitals-from a high of 40 institutions down to the present six hospitals. In the intervening years, however, hospital insurance was introduced so all citizens are entitled to hospital care, including WVA recipients, and DVA retains financial responsibility only for the treatment of disability pensioners and for their pensioned disability.
Finally, DVA hospitals have become, essentially, institutions where 90 per cent of care is extended care and fewer than 10 per cent of patients are entitled pensioners. The operation of such hospitals is becoming increasingly more difficult in terms of quality of care. The vast majority of the patients now in our hospitals are a provincial responsibility, in the sense that they are covered by hospital insurance.
Because of the conditions I have described, the government decided in 1963 that active steps should be taken to transfer the remaining DVA hospitals, with the expectation that they would be integrated into community health systems.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in the debate on Bill C-22, being part of the legislation arising from the ways and means budget motions which allows for wide ranging debate. Hopefully we will hear from the minister what he feels is in store for the country. Certainly there is widespread unease about the economic status of Canada today, which has been manifested by the fall in the value of the dollar. Quite apart from the coming to power a couple of Mondays ago of Mr. Rene Levesque whose avowed intention is to break up the country into component parts. The financial situation of Canada is more serious than it has been for a long time.
Before embarking upon a general discussion of the bill I should like to make a couple of observations about it. It is mainly a housekeeping bill and is of no great significance. Secondly, representations have been made to me by knowledgeable accountants and heavy equipment operators that the change in the depreciation allowances for heavy equipment is of concern to them. No doubt this provision was used as a tax haven by some people. A person could buy a bulldozer for $80,000, rent it out at $1,000 a month and write off a $30,000 loss. However, there are many contractors who made genuine use of the provision.
The contracting industry is a rather risky one. I can remember some years ago a contractor built his house right beside mine and mentioned he was going to put it in his wife's name. When I asked why, he said he had been sold out by the bailiff twice already on Christmas Eve and he was not going to allow it to happen again. There is no doubt contracting is a risky business. High depreciation has been a useful tool that has enabled some independent contractors to continue in business, and although there has been abuse by certain high income people I think it behooves the minister to allow contractors to continue to make genuine use of the provision and to retain the same approximate level of depreciation that has existed in the past.
I should also like to say a few words about registered retirement savings plans. I am not enamoured of the idea that tax free registered retirement plans are necessarily a good thing for this country in the long run. Raising the ceiling to the proposed levels is in line with the inflation rate, and outwardly it appears as though it is going to aid the economy by aiding savings. But this form of savings has certain drawbacks. First of all, it is a saving of tax which means that a good part of the saving really belongs to the government. If the tax system were functioning correctly, these tax free savings would not be



December 2, 1976
Income Tax
necessary. It would not be necessary to bribe our people into saving money, a good portion of which really belongs to the government.
What happens to this money, Mr. Speaker? It is collected into huge holdings which are managed by just a few managers. Naturally they must manage these funds to the best of their ability since they represent the savings and pensions of their clients, so they tend to invest only in blue chip companies or government bonds. This dries up the normal financial flow that might go into venture capital and into more risky businesses.
I think the pension retirement plan study that was conducted in the United States was very interesting. It showed that over the last 25 years most of the major pension companies were owned by pension funds. When we heard about corporate bums a few years ago, in many instances this really would have meant corporate pension plans which, as I say, were owned by registered retirement funds. I do not think this is necessarily a good thing. It is something we will have to consider in the future in order to prevent large blocks of capital being in the hands of a few managers and contained as they must be by government regulations.
I should like to turn now to our own political and economic situation. Even before the Quebec election economic problems seemed to descend on us severely. For almost two years in a row we have had a foreign trade deficit of upwards of $7 billion. One has only to place this in perspective to realize that in a similar situation in the United States this would have meant a deficit of something in the order of $70 billion. Only a few years ago there was great alarm in United States financial circles at a deficit of $15 billion or $20 billion, which would have respresented only $2 billion for us, so we can see what serious trouble this poses for us. We have been able to contain this because of a huge inflow of debt borrowed by the giant corporations. We should not blame the private corporations as much as institutions such as Quebec Hydro, Manitoba Hydro, and the Potash Corporation of Saskatchewan which are involved in the major cost of borrowing through the provincial governments in the political field.
I am well aware that this large foreign trade deficit really is the result of economic forces at work within our country. I do think this vast borrowing abroad has been instituted by political decisions of provincial governments and provincial utilities to undertake projects on a grandiose scale in many instances far beyond the potential of this country to cope with at least over a shorter term.
What is the point of the Saskatchewan government buying potash companies at, as I understand, a good price, and raising the money in New York, to be taken by the American owned potash company which is drilling for potash in the continental United States across the border which, if successful, will diminish the market for the Saskatchewan product? It would seem that it would have made more sense had Saskatchewan developed another potash mine.

We have heard much in the past about foreign investment. A few years ago the nationalists said that foreign investment should be in the form of debt equity and not ownership. While we seem to have effectively cured that problem, more investment money is leaving the country than is coming in and we find that whether it is debt equity or actual ownership with dividend payments, the cost is the same. When the economy of the country is low, foreign dividend payments reflect this but interest payments must be made regardless of the state of the economy. As anyone who has been involved in business understands, it is far better to have a partner with an investment when business is poor than to have a mortgage held by a hard taskmaster.
Government spending clearly is out of hand. Canadians have been spending far too much. They have been merely mortgaging the future to spend for today. The programs set in motion in the 1960's in respect of health, welfare, and education are now realizing their full cost. We now realize that what the country can afford is not what people like. With our social programs we have been living on champagne tastes with a beer economy. In recent months we have been struck by a comparison of United States and Canadian costs. To highlight the difference I might point out there was an item in the Winnipeg newspapers to the effect that high prices had sent American tourists home screeching in horror. This, as usual, was attributed by a government official to excess charging by the hotel industry in Winnipeg. But the hotel industry came back and pointed out the very much lower level of taxation and wage structure the American industry enjoys.
I think there is a fairly reasonable explanation for the large difference in wage structure between the two industries with somewhat comparable productivity. In fact Americans pay far more for their social services out of their own pockets while in Canada such costs are collected whenever a transaction occurs. Ideally perhaps for the individual the Canadian welfare structure is good, but with the U.S. economic structure he then would have the best of both worlds.

People who worry about such things have long known that the Canadian dollar is overpriced. And now that it is declining at an alarming rate, some wiseacres (who, historically, are more often wrong than right), predict it may continue to decline to 92.5 cents American.

Mr. Speaker, we are debating a bill making some changes to the Income Tax Act. I suggest that this country is undoubtedly facing greater problems than any we have faced in the history of Canada, except during the two world wars. We are facing the problem of inflation which is hitting people on lower incomes in an extremely pernicious way, and we are facing the problem of unemployment, with which I will deal at some length in a little while, the kind of unemployment which just a few years ago we in all parties agreed would never take place again. We thought we had learnt from the experience of the last 30 years that mass unemployment was no longer necessary.
We thought just a few years ago-and the thought was accepted by all parties-that we could have full employment, and that full employment was in the neighbourhood of 4 per cent unemployment. Now the economists, particularly those around the Economic Council of Canada, have begun to rationalize full employment as being considerably more than 4 per cent unemployment, and they give all kinds of reasons why full employment is reached when there is unemployment in the neighbourhood of 6 per cent. They say that now, because we have over 7 per cent unemployment, and I suppose that if unemployment gets higher, as it undoubtedly will given the present government's policies, next year they will be saying that full employment is when unemployment is in the neighbourhood of 7 per cent.
Then, of course, we are facing the threat to the unity of this country through the election of a government in Quebec committed to the separation of that province from the Canada which we have known for over 100 years. We have to ask ourselves how we arrived at this situation, and if we look at these questions seriously we will see that we have arrived at

One of the issues which 1 suspect hon. members in all parties have been hearing about from their constituents is this question of the future of the retirement savings program which requires at age 70 that an annuity be purchased with the proceeds of the retirement fund. Indeed the consumers association of Canada has been particularly active in this regard. As an interim response I think I would have to remind those interested in this question that the registered retirement savings plan provisions of the Income Tax Act were put in the act in an effort to give those who are self-employed, or who are not entitled to the benefits of a registered pension plan, the same opportunity as participants in a pension plan to deduct from their taxable income from year to year amounts they would set aside for retirement.
The underlying policy is that it is in the interest not only of the employers and employees, but also the community in a broader sense, that individuals should make provision in a systematic way for their retirement years. Before the registered retirement plan provisions in respect of income tax were brought into being there was not that opportunity for people who were not participants in a company plan. Therefore the present provisions of the Income Tax Act are intended to try to place the self-employed-and that of course includes more people than the self-employed, but that is a form of shorthand if I might refer to them in that way-in the same position as pension plan participants so that they would be able to take periodic deductions and be in the same position as most pension plan recipients of having the right to a periodic payment of income rather than a lump sum payment upon their retirement from active employment. It is for this reason the provisions of the law were created requiring that the proceeds be put into an annuity pension which would be paid

out to the individual as time goes on. In a sense, unless one did that, the self-employed would then have a tax benefit which those in company pension plans would not enjoy.
The argument has been made-and there has been extensive debate on both sides of the question-either that the annuity requirement is a bonanza for the life companies, or conversely that on the part of the life companies in representative cases the individual stands to gain over the longer run by putting his funds into an annuity in this particular way. At this point I come down on neither one side nor the other of the argument, except to say this will be assessed within the context of the retirement income study and that we would give attention at that time to meeting the concern expressed, but bearing in mind at the same time the importance of equity as between people on company pension plans and those who have this provision for savings for their own retirement.
The hon. member for Edmonton West also drew attention to the specific problem with regard to the increase that is involved in the R.R.S.P. deductions, that is to say, the increase in the contribution limit to $5,500 will benefit only those having between $20,000 and $27,500 a year of earned income. As I understand the hon. gentleman's proposal, it was with respect to those 55 years or more who had not been contributing to a retirement pension plan and that there would be no percentage limit but just the $5,500, and that others would be entitled to a higher percentage.
I would have to say there is no magic in the figure of 20 per cent. It is one that has seemed to be reasonable. A practical consideration of course is that there are few people earning $10,000, $12,000 or even $15,000 a year who can use the full 20 per cent limit. It is difficult for them to save that much. It can be argued that an increase in the percentage would incline to favour those with an investment income who could live off their investment income and shelter more of their earned income in this way. That is the argument in respect of this particular group. As the hon. member knows, one of the great difficulties in creating any monetary crossover point is that naturally there are feelings of inequity on both sides of the frontier created. I am prepared to consider that, but at the moment I am inclined to think the provision we have left in the law is a reasonable restraint.
The hon. member made some comments with regard to the payout requirements under the charities provisions, in particular some of the requirements of the charities provisions with regard to capital payout. I know that the 5 percent capital payout is still regarded as being rather tough by some private foundations, but we feel that with the transitional rule that is provided the requirement can be fair. I do not know whether I should really deal with that in extenso at this point, or deal with it perhaps when we get to the amendments in respect of the charities. I think it might be better to defer any exhaustive comment until that point.
I should like to thank members for their contributions. We will now be moving to the clause by clause consideration. I might indicate that we have on hand a number of amendments to the bill which we will bring forward to deal with particular
December 2, 1976

comments that have been received on certain aspects of the bill. I will ask one of my colleagues to bring these forward when we come to those particular points.

Frankly, I do not think this is right. The employee in a big union, such as in the CNR, running or operating trains, has no say so in this matter. It is a condition of employment, and this applies not only to the CNR but to many other collective agreements in organizations with many employees. The employee is bound under a variety of formulas. He either goes along with the crowd or he quits his employment. The contribution is paid into the registered pension plan solely by the employer, and the employee is barred
Income Tax
by the rules of the Income Tax Act from making any contribution to the registered retirement savings plan.
I should like to hear the minister confirm whether or not 1 am correct in my interpretation and, if so, what would be the rationale in maintaining this disability, because I maintain that the rationale of the registered pension plan and the R.R.S.P. is the encouragement of a great cross section of workers to provide something for their retirement. There are incentives by way of deferred tax on both these plans so that the individual does not prescribe to a socialist philosophy of earning all he can, spending all he can, and at the age of 65 holding out the pockets of his trousers and saying, "I have spent everything, now the state will look after me".
I think the philosophy which is recognized in the Income Tax Act under R.R.S.P.'s and under registered pension plans is that however low an individual's income may be, as a result of the contributions paid by the employer and by him there is provision for some savings for his retirement. To me this is the greatest of the social objectives that we can have in so far as the state is concerned, rather than the state trying to induce the individual to spend everything and then come to the gate at the age of 65-or whatever may be the variation in so far as spouses are concerned-and saying, "Here I am, I am devoid of everything but the clothes in which I stand. Now support me in the style to which I would aspire". That philosophy is prevalent among far too many people today in Canada.
I will ask the minister to say whether I am right or wrong in my technical application of the Income Tax Act and, if 1 am right, could he give his views as to why he insists that the act shall continue as it is presently designed?

Any plan to inspire people to save for years when they will no longer be working is beneficial, and so I welcome programs to encourage people to save. Many in the House will remember that during the last war there was a program under which people could put money away, and that money was used for the benefit of the country. It was not necessarily used for the benefit of the citizen individually, but it was of benefit to the country because Canadians became involved in financing their country. I think we should use every means available to us to get people to do this because there seems to be a very widespread feeling today that we might as well spend what we have, eat, drink and be merry, and let tomorrow take care of itself. This is a very dangerous philosophy, therefore I encourage the minister to look further into registered retirement savings.
The point I want to bring to the attention of the House is that at the present time many people are concerned that when they become 71 they will either have to take the money out of their registered retirement savings plans and pay tax on it as of that date, or turn it into an annuity with an insurance company. subtopic: INDUSTRY-CANADAIR-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF DOCUMENTS AUTHORIZING LOAN GUARANTEE AND SPECIFYING ORDERS
INDUSTRY-CANADAIR-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF DOCUMENTS AUTHORIZING LOAN GUARANTEE AND SPECIFYING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when one takes into consideration that the Government of Canada has guaranteed a loan of $50 million of the Canadian taxpayers' money to Canadair, I for one find it very questionable that the government refuses to supply parliament with pertinent information with regard to Canadair.
In particular, Mr. Speaker, I am referring to my question of November 2 to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) in which I requested that the minister table the document whereby the government authorizes the loan guarantee. That was not done, and as Canadair is now owned by the taxpayers of Canada, and as the board of directors has a majority of senior civil servants presumably representing the taxpayers' interests, I feel the government owes parliament some answers on Canadair.
With $50 million of public funds invested in Canadair, the government has an obligation to come clean and state just what its plans and expectations are for Canadair. There are several matters with regard to the LearStar that must be raised.
Fundamental to the entire matter is the basic decision of the government to purchase Canadair. Having made this questionable decision, and since it has not divested itself of this establishment, the government faces the inevitable problem of having a major plant facility in a depressed industry. Out of this rises the question, if the government's investment in Canadair is a "make work" program for the Montreal area then why doesn't the government designate it as such, and different criteria should be applied? The Liberal government has squandered far too much of the taxpayers' dollars on schemes in the past and should be accountable.
Mr. Lear in his public statement on the Canadair program said that the market could reach 2,500 aircraft over a ten year

period. I have consulted with aircraft experts, and they find that very questionable. There has not been a civilian jet aircraft that has sold anywhere near this number, and the most successful jet aircraft ever produced, the Boeing 727, has approximately 1,200 in existence. Fred Kearns, president of Canadair, was obviously conscious of this fact when he stated that 1,000 might be a more reasonable number. Even that figure is similarly optimistic and I note that the minister has referred to between 250 and 300 aircraft over a five to seven year period.
You know, Mr. Speaker, the sale of 300 aircraft in the $3 million price range would be a successful program, but there would have to be a highly successful marketing program. If you look at the record of the Gulfstream Two, which is the obvious competitor for the LearStar, this aircraft has established a strong position in the market but sales are well below the 200 level.
As far as the commuter service area is concerned, based on the information I have, I do not believe that there is a market not presently being serviced by either turbo-prop aircraft or existing twin jets such as the VFW-614. It would seem that the government is in a sense competing with itself because the major thrust of the De Havilland Dash 7 was directed toward the commuter short haul market and with the type of stage lengths being considered there is no particular advantage to jet speeds. In fact the turbo-prop aircraft is less costly to operate at these stage lengths than the jet aircraft, particularly in the area of fuel consumption.
The major market for this aircraft must rest in the executive aircraft field and I would think that if the probable maximum market is between 200 and 300 aircraft over a ten year period then one has to question the economic basis for the investment. In an article that appeared in Le Soleil dated September 14, 1976, it would appear that the requirements for the program could total $150 million. At that level Canadair would have to sell 500 aircraft just to recover the investment let alone cost of money over the intervening period.
The government is being naive in suggesting that the only funds that it will provide are a guarantee of $50 million. We all know that if additional funds are necessary they will be provided since the government would otherwise be faced with having to close down the facilities or meet the guarantees that it has undertaken.
In light of the conflicting figures on projected LearStar sales, as well as other questions in relation to Canadair, the time has come for the government to quit hiding behind the cloak of secrecy and refer this matter before parliament. Secrecy under these circumstances should in no way be tolerated because tax dollars are involved. 1 contend that the proper course of action is either to refer this matter to the Standing Committee on Industry, Trade and Commerce or to establish a special committee to delve into the Canadair program. In the meantime it is absolutely imperative that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce table all the pertinent documents related to Canadair.
December 2, 1976

With $50 million committed to Canadair there certainly are a lot of unanswered questions. Certainly in transactions between firms in the private sector no profit motivated company would enter into such a large transaction without reasonable assurances that it was a wise venture. The Canadian taxpayers expect the same from the government and would like to know what kind of a venture Canadair is.
In the final analysis the only real hope that the taxpayer has is that the government will divest itself of Canadair as soon as possible. If Canadair is really a potentially profitable operation then one would anticipate increased interest by the private sector in purchasing Canadair. In the meantime the government should start revealing the true information with regard to Canadair.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member referred to the question he asked, and I would draw his attention to the words of the minister in reply. He said:
Last Friday in Montreal 1 held a press conference on this matter during which I gave all the information. We guaranteed a loan of $50 million, the government of Quebec a loan of $20 million and the balance of the program to be financed through two Canadian banks.
I should like to explain the matter further for the benefit of the hon. member. Canadair estimate that it will require to borrow up to a maximum of $128 million in 1979 for the LearStar 600 program. The funds will be used in both the development and production phases of the program to finance the work in process and inventory build-up prior to delivery of the first aircraft. Present arrangements are for the $128 million to be provided by a consortium of two Canadian chartered banks. The federal government will guarantee $50 million of the loan and the province of Quebec will guarantee a further $20 million. The balance of the financing, $58 million, will be secured by a pledge of Canadair's assets.
The LearStar program is recognized by the federal government to be a relatively high risk venture. However, the potential benefits to Canada in terms of exports, employment, technology gains and return on investment are considered to be sufficiently high to warrant supporting the program.
In terms of anticipated benefits, a market for 250 aircraft, with an export value of $950,000,000, is forecast. The program should create 1,500 jobs at Canadair and a further 1,500 at other facilities in Canada. Canadair will gain access to the advanced technology in airframes and engines and will earn a very satisfactory return on investment if the program goes according to plan. Independent consultants retained by the department have evaluated the market and the estimated program costs and have indicated that Canadair's estimates are, in their opinion, soundly based.
Firm orders with deposits have now been received for 58 aircraft from major corporations, and additional orders are expected before the end of the year. The present order backlog for LearStar aircraft is about $300 million.

subtopic: INDUSTRY-CANADAIR-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF DOCUMENTS AUTHORIZING LOAN GUARANTEE AND SPECIFYING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the report of the Auditor General, in the normal course of events documents the infinite capacity of the government for misal-locating the taxpayers' money, has reached beyond a comedy of errors to reveal a drama played on an international stage which is at times shadowy, at times sinister. The actors I want to deal with in this drama are two powerful Crown corporations, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Polysar Corporation.
The AECL connection concerned a $15.3 million commission payment made to a company called United Development Inc. which had acted as the corporation's sales agent in negotiating the recent nuclear sale to South Korea. Of this payment, $5.1 million was commission on the sale and $8 million was billed as expenses for which the accounting was, in the restrained prose of the Auditor General's report, inadequate. In addition to these nebulous expenses, which included $2.5 million to consultants, there was also included a $2 million advance payment on a post services contract which calls for minimum payments of $175,000 by AECL every three months for what could well be the next eight years.
I raised the question of the payments for the services being rendered with respect to this so-called commission paid to Mr. Sol Eisenberg, who apparently is a principal of this particular company, hoping that I would get some information from the minister. The reason I bring it up tonight is that unfortunately from my point of view, and I think from the point of view of shedding light on this particular topic, the minister again persisted in evading the question by sloughing it off on the basis that it is being answered in another place at another time.
Unfortunately I have to point out to the House that the minister was not absolutely correct in his assertion that the question has been answered. We are still in the dark with respect to the services being rendered for these particular payments. In fact during the course of the committee deliberations it was suggested that the Auditor General travel to Tel Aviv to investigate the books and discuss the nature of the services rendered with Mr. Eisenberg. But Mr. Macdonell refused to accept this suggestion because limitations were placed upon the terms upon which he could investigate the books of Mr. Eisenberg. He said that he was prepared to go to Tel Aviv only if there was an assurance that he could learn the nature of the services and expenses that have been billed for. He also wanted to know the nature of the post services contract for which AECL agreed to pay up to $5 million, $2 million of which has already been paid.
I think the government does Atomic Energy of Canada Limited a great disservice by continuing to avoid answering questions and by not taking the initiative and getting to the bottom of it, coming clean with the Canadian people, and particularly with the House of Commons, as to what precisely

December 2, 1976
Adjournment Debate
is going on. I hope that the parliamentary secretary will be able to enlighten us as to what services are being provided for this massive amount of money that is in the nature of a commission.
The Auditor General is a respected servant of parliament; he has expressed concern, and I think we owe a duty to him and to the people of Canada to have the situation explained by the government, hopefully by the parliamentary secretary tonight. As long as the question remains unanswered there will be continued speculation as to the nature of these payments and, whether the government likes it or not, there will be the suggestion that there is something very unusual happening, leading to the further speculation that there is something improper.
It is not members of the opposition who are causing this speculation to be made. I think when people are not given the full facts, as very often they are not by this government, it is only human nature to tend to suspect there is something wrong. If I may be permitted to give advice to the government, I would ask it please to let us know precisely what services were involved in this particular transaction; and also I ask the parliamentary secretary to explain tonight whether or not under this particular arrangement with Mr. Eisenberg we in Canada will be faced with a total expenditure, not of $15.3 million but something in excess of $20 million, for services that have not been verified as yet.
If we are in fact paying these quarterly payments of $175,000 until at least 1980, in my estimation this means that the total amount that will be expended in respect of the commission to Mr. Eisenberg and his company in connection with this transaction will exceed $20 million. I hope the parliamentary secretary will be in a position to explain why the minister seemed to indicate that would not be the case. If there is an explanation I would like to hear it tonight.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: INDUSTRY-CANADAIR-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF DOCUMENTS AUTHORIZING LOAN GUARANTEE AND SPECIFYING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on reading questions the hon. member addressed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) in this House last Friday, November 26, it is evident to me that the member was under some misapprehension. I refer in particular to the question which indicated it was the member's impression that under the renegotiated contract AECL might ultimately pay its agent in the Republic of Korea in excess of $20 million, or more than was provided for in the original contract.
The minister answered the question by stating that it had been made quite clear before the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works that the renegotiated contract was for a lesser amount than the original contract. In case the member himself is still not quite clear on the matter I should like to elaborate.
The original contract provided for the payment of $20 million. Under the renegotiated agreement, the amount cannot
exceed $18.4 million. The latter includes a provision for postcontract services, payments to be made quarterly for expenses incurred, to a total not to exceed a fixed amount, namely, $5,142,392 over the entire performance and warranty period.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: INDUSTRY-CANADAIR-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF DOCUMENTS AUTHORIZING LOAN GUARANTEE AND SPECIFYING ORDERS

subtopic: INDUSTRY-CANADAIR-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF DOCUMENTS AUTHORIZING LOAN GUARANTEE AND SPECIFYING ORDERS
speechtext:
You have a choice. There is a provision in this contract whereby, should AECL question any invoice, AECL shall nevertheless pay in respect of such quarter $175,000. In other words, this is not, as the member seemed to think, an open-ended contract.
The hon. member also wanted to know what would constitute the post-contract services AECL would receive from the agent. As this House is well aware, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has asked, and the chairman and members have agreed, that the Public Accounts Committee examine at an early date AECL's employment of agents for the purpose of effecting power reactor sales in the Republic of Korea and Argentina. So far three committee meetings have taken place. Because of the great number of questions put to the Auditor General we have not yet had an opportunity to examine either the minister or the officials of AECL. Nevertheless, I do not think it would be redundant to answer the question now, and in fact it might help to dispel some of the uncertainty that now exists.
Throughout the performance and warranty period of the contract between AECL and the Korea Electric Company- approximately seven years-the agent will provide services which will include first, assistance in getting AECL's office and personnel established in Korea; second, assistance with the entry and handling of all goods imported for the job, the value amounting to well over $100 million over the construction period; third, assistance, as necessary with local subcontracts for labour, material and services; fourth, advice on Korean laws and regulations affecting the execution of the main contract; fifth, commercial assistance to AECL in respect of dealing with the customer concerning changes in the scope of work and the provision of spare parts; sixth, provide experienced staff in Korea and elsewhere as necessary to perform these functions.
These are services that are now foreseen at a very early stage of the project. They are more in the form of a framework than a detailed description. Undoubtedly there will be others which AECL will require and the agent will provide, under the terms of the agreement.
The hon. member has asked why the services to be provided by the agent could not be supplied by the purchaser. I believe the outline I have given helps to answer that question. In any event, these services are of a kind that are either the responsibility of the supplier or are in the suppliers' interest. If they were not provided by an agent, they would have to be obtained from other organizations. This is the only way to do it. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
